source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. V (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio capituli primi: Arphaxad itaque rex Medorum subjugaverat gentes multas
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: Now Arphaxad king of the Medes had brought many nations under his dominions

paras.t: Beneficium magnificæ liberationis concessæ filiis Israel per venerabilem viduam Judith, in hoc libro describitur: ideo præmittuntur præambula quædam ad declarandum, qualiter facta sit liberatio illa.
paras.en: In this book is described the benefit of the magnificent deliverance granted to the children of Israel through the venerable widow Judith: and so certain preliminaries are set first, to make clear how that deliverance came about.

paras.t: Arphaxad itaque rex Medorum subjugaverat gentes multas imperio suo; quia non sufficit suæ ambitioni atque tyrannidi regnare in Media, sed ad monarchiam quamdam adspirans, multas provincias per armorum violentiam subdidit sibi: nec erat hæres regni Medorum, sed natus ex populo regni illius. Cyrus quippe rex Persarum, victo Astyage avo suo rege Persarum, ipsum Astyagem tractavit humane, dans ei regnum Hyrcanorum, id est Parthorum, et Dario fratri matris suæ, filio Astyagis, dedit regnum Medorum sub spe redeundi ad illud, seu rehabendi id ipsum: quod et factum est. Mortuo autem Cyro, Arphaxad Medus partem regni illius sibi attraxit, ut tandem toti Mediæ præsideret. Atque in urbe Ecbatanis nomine surgens, urbem illam vehementer auxit, reparavit, munivit, et quasi inexpugnabiliter confortavit muris, portis et turribus, præsertim ad resistendum filio Cyri regis: prout hæc in Scholastica historia plenius recitantur. Hinc subditur: Et ipse ædificavit civitatem potentissimam, quam appellavit Ecbatanis; quam dicitur ædificasse, quia præfato modo eam reparavit, auxit et melioravit. Juxta quem sensum Nabuchodonosor fertur dixisse: Nonne hæc est Babylon magna, quam ego ædificavi in domum regni? quum tamen Babylon diu ante fuerit ædificata, quum scriptum sit in Genesi: Fuit autem principium regni ejus, scilicet ipsius Nemrod, Babylon et Arach.
paras.en: [[1:1|Now Arphaxad king of the Medes had brought many nations under his dominions|Arphaxad itaque rex Medorum subjugaverat gentes multas imperio suo]]: because it was not enough for his ambition and tyranny to reign in Media, but, aspiring to a kind of monarchy [that is, rule over all the kingdoms], he subdued many provinces to himself by force of arms. Nor was he heir of the kingdom of the Medes, but born of the people of that kingdom. For Cyrus king of the Persians, having overcome Astyages his grandfather, king of the Persians [so the text; Astyages was king of the Medes], treated Astyages himself humanely, giving him the kingdom of the Hyrcanians, that is, of the Parthians; and to Darius, his mother's brother, the son of Astyages, he gave the kingdom of the Medes, in the hope that it would return to him, or that he would have it again: which also came about. But when Cyrus was dead, Arphaxad the Mede drew part of that kingdom to himself, so that in the end he ruled over all Media. And rising up in the city named Ecbatana, he greatly enlarged that city, repaired it, fortified it, and strengthened it with walls, gates and towers so as to be almost impregnable, above all in order to resist the son of King Cyrus: as these things are related more fully in the Scholastic History [of Peter Comestor]. Hence it is added: [[1:1|and he built a very strong city, which he called Ecbatana|Et ipse ædificavit civitatem potentissimam, quam appellavit Ecbatanis]]; which he is said to have built because he repaired, enlarged and improved it in the way described. In this sense Nabuchodonosor is said to have said: [[Dan 4:27|Is not this the great Babylon, which I have built, to be the seat of the kingdom|Nonne hæc est Babylon magna, quam ego ædificavi in domum regni?]]? though Babylon had been built long before, since it is written in Genesis: [[Gen 10:10|And the beginning of his kingdom|Fuit autem principium regni ejus]], that is, of Nemrod, [[Gen 10:10|was Babylon, and Arach|Babylon et Arach]].

paras.t: Arphaxad itaque urbem illam construxit ex lapidibus quadratis, ut muri, turres, portæ, et domus exsisterent fortiores, et sectis, ut essent pulchriores. Fecit muros ejus in altitudine cubitorum septuaginta, et in latitudine cubitorum triginta; turres vero ejus posuit in altitudine cubitorum centum. Quod totum ministerio gravissimo gentium quas subjugaverat, fecit, sicut et Nabuchodonosor Babylonem, cum qua urbs ista Ecbatanis similitudinem habuit magnam; sed ad ipsius æqualitatem et excellentiam non pervenit, quum muri Babylonis legantur fuisse altitudinis centum cubitorum, et quinquaginta in latitudine, turres vero ducentorum cubitorum. Per quadrum vero earum, latus utrumque vicenorum pedum spatio tendebatur, id est, utrumque latus turrium per quadrum cubitorum protendebatur spatio pedum viginti ultra latitudinem murorum. Nam turres erant figuræ quadrangularis ad æquales angulos, et muri turrium extendebant se per spatium viginti pedum, tam extra urbem quam infra, ultra latitudinem murorum. Posuitque portas ejus in altitudine turrium: ita quod erant centum cubitorum, quemadmodum turres, ut littera videtur sonare, quamvis aliqui aliter dicant.
paras.en: So Arphaxad built that city of [[1:2|stones squared|lapidibus quadratis]], so that the walls, towers, gates and houses might be stronger, [[1:2|and hewed|et sectis]], so that they might be more beautiful. [[1:2|he made the walls thereof seventy cubits broad, and thirty cubits high|Fecit muros ejus in altitudine cubitorum septuaginta, et in latitudine cubitorum triginta]] [Denis, with the Vulgate, reads *seventy cubits high and thirty broad*]; [[1:2|and the towers thereof he made a hundred cubits high|turres vero ejus posuit in altitudine cubitorum centum]]. All this he did by the heaviest labour of the nations he had subdued, as Nabuchodonosor also built Babylon, which this city of Ecbatana closely resembled; but it did not come up to its equal or its excellence, since the walls of Babylon are read to have been a hundred cubits high and fifty broad, and its towers two hundred cubits. [[1:2|But on the square of them, each side was extended the space of twenty feet|Per quadrum vero earum, latus utrumque vicenorum pedum spatio tendebatur]], that is, each side of the towers, on the square, stretched out the space of twenty feet beyond the breadth of the walls. For the towers were of a four-sided figure with equal angles, and the walls of the towers stretched out the space of twenty feet beyond the breadth of the walls, both outside the city and within. [[1:3|And he made the gates thereof according to the height of the towers|Posuitque portas ejus in altitudine turrium]]: so that they were a hundred cubits, like the towers, as the letter seems to say, though some say otherwise.

paras.t: Et gloriabatur inaniter, quasi potens, id est tam superbe et præsumptuose, ac si a se ipso habuisset potentiam, sicut in Ezechiele Dominus loquitur Pharaoni: Audi, Pharao, draco magne, qui dicis, Meus est fluvius, et ego feci me ipsum. Vel, Quasi potens, quia utique potens fuit, sed non tam singulariter ut putavit. In potentia exercitus sui copiosi, et in gloria quadrigarum suarum, id est in multitudine, fortitudine, ac eminentia suorum curruum bellicorum: quia frequenter consueverunt olim pugnare stando in curribus, prout ex libris Josue et Judicum innotescit.
paras.en: [[1:4|And he gloried|Et gloriabatur]] vainly, [[1:4|as a mighty one|quasi potens]], that is, as proudly and presumptuously as if he had had his might from himself, as the Lord speaks to Pharao in Ezechiel: Hear, Pharao, [[Ezech 29:3|thou great dragon|draco magne]], who sayest, [[Ezech 29:3|The river is mine, and I made myself|Meus est fluvius, et ego feci me ipsum]]. Or, *as a mighty one*, because he was indeed mighty, but not so uniquely as he thought. [[1:4|in the force of his army|In potentia exercitus sui]], a numerous one, [[1:4|and in the glory of his chariots|et in gloria quadrigarum suarum]], that is, in the number, strength and excellence of his war chariots: for in old times they were often wont to fight standing in chariots, as is known from the books of Josue and Judges[[Jos 11:4||]][[Judg 1:19||]][[Judg 4:3||]] [the margin, partly unreadable, seems to give Jos. xi, 4; Judg. i, 19; iv, 3].

paras.t: Anno igitur duodecimo regni sui, non præfati Arphaxad, sed duodecimo anno regni Cambysis filii Cyri, de quo subditur, Nabuchodonosor rex Assyriorum: qui alio nomine dictus est Cambyses, atque in Esdra nominatur Artaxerxes vel Assuerus, qui regnabat in Ninive civitate magna, quam ante jam Chaldæi destruxerunt, sed postea exstitit reparata. Porro Cyrus rex adhuc vivens, filio suo Cambysi tradidit regnum Assyriorum, cujus regni metropolis Ninive erat. Regnavit autem Cambyses in monarchia solummodo octo annis. Idcirco, quod hic dicitur de duodecimo anno regni ejus, accipitur per inclusionem annorum quibus regnavit, Cyro monarcha patre suo adhuc vivente. Pugnavit contra Arphaxad, et obtinuit, id est vicit, eum in campo magno qui appellatur Ragau, in quo tam magni exercitus poterant collocari, circa Euphraten et Tigrim, id est inter duo flumina illa, et Jadason, in campo Erioch regis Elicorum.
paras.en: [[1:5|Now in the twelfth year of his reign|Anno igitur duodecimo regni sui]]: not of the aforesaid Arphaxad, but in the twelfth year of the reign of Cambyses son of Cyrus, of whom it is added: [[1:5|Nabuchodonosor king of the Assyrians|Nabuchodonosor rex Assyriorum]], who by another name was called Cambyses, and in Esdras is named Artaxerxes or Assuerus[[1 Esd 4:6||]][[1 Esd 4:7||]], [[1:5|who reigned in Ninive the great city|qui regnabat in Ninive civitate magna]], which the Chaldeans had already destroyed before, but which was afterwards rebuilt. Now King Cyrus, while still alive, handed over to his son Cambyses the kingdom of the Assyrians, whose capital was Ninive. And Cambyses reigned in the monarchy only eight years. Therefore what is said here of the twelfth year of his reign is taken as including the years in which he reigned while Cyrus his father, the monarch, was still alive. [[1:5|fought against Arphaxad and overcame him|Pugnavit contra Arphaxad, et obtinuit, id est vicit, eum]] (*obtinuit*, that is, conquered him) in [[1:6|the great plain which is called Ragua|campo magno qui appellatur Ragau]], in which such great armies could be drawn up, [[1:6|about the Euphrates, and the Tigris|circa Euphraten et Tigrim]], that is, between those two rivers, [[1:6|and the Jadason|et Jadason]], [[1:6|in the plain of Erioch the king of the Elicians|in campo Erioch regis Elicorum]].

paras.t: Tunc exaltatum est regnum Nabuchodonosor hujus, tanto adversario suo dejecto, et cor ejus elevatum est in superbiam plus quam ante, non Deo, sed robori suo triumphum illum adscribens, quum tamen omnipotens mundi Rector per ipsum tanquam per suum flagellum castigasset et occidisset violentum illum, tyrannicumque Arphaxad: secundum quod in Isaia rex Assyriorum Sennacherib, vocatur virga furoris Dei et baculus ejus. Et misit ad omnes qui habitabant in Cilicia et Damasco, metropoli regni Syriæ, juxta illud Isaiæ, Caput Syriæ Damascus, et Libano, et ad gentes quæ sunt in Carmelo et Cedar, et inhabitantes Galilæam, in campo magno Esdrelon, et ad omnes qui erant in Samaria, et trans flumen Jordanem usque ad Jerusalem, et omnem terram Jesse.
paras.en: [[1:7|Then was the kingdom of Nabuchodonosor exalted|Tunc exaltatum est regnum Nabuchodonosor]], that is, of this Nabuchodonosor, now that so great an adversary of his had been cast down, [[1:7|and his heart was elevated|et cor ejus elevatum est]] in pride more than before, ascribing that triumph not to God but to his own strength; though in truth the almighty Ruler of the world had chastised and slain that violent and tyrannical Arphaxad by him as by his scourge: as in Isaias the king of the Assyrians, Sennacherib, is called the rod of God's fury and his staff[[Is 10:5||]]. [[1:7|and he sent to all that dwelt in Cilicia and Damascus|Et misit ad omnes qui habitabant in Cilicia et Damasco]], the capital of the kingdom of Syria, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 7:8|the head of Syria is Damascus|Caput Syriæ Damascus]], [[1:7|and Libanus|et Libano]], and [[1:8|to the nations that are in Carmelus, and Cedar|ad gentes quæ sunt in Carmelo et Cedar]], [[1:8|and to the inhabitants of Galilee in the great plain of Asdrelon|et inhabitantes Galilæam, in campo magno Esdrelon]], and [[1:9|to all that were in Samaria|ad omnes qui erant in Samaria]], [[1:9|and beyond the river Jordan even to Jerusalem, and all the land of Jesse|et trans flumen Jordanem usque ad Jerusalem, et omnem terram Jesse]].

paras.t: Circa hoc oritur quæstio duplex. Prima, quoniam Cyrus pater istius fuit monarcha: unde ait, Omnia regna terræ dedit mihi Deus cœli: monarchia autem nondum ablata fuit Medis et Persis; ergo Cambyses imperavit jam et præfuit omnibus regnis his. Secunda est, quoniam Samaritani leguntur in libro primo Esdræ favisse huic regi, ad quorum petitionem prohibuit templi reparationem, quod pater ejus licentiavit reædificari. Iste est namque Artaxerxes, cui scripserunt Samaritani, memores salis quod in palatio comederant regis. Ad primum horum aliqui dicunt, quod Cambyses seu Nabuchodonosor iste petiit a præfatis regnis et populis tributa multo graviora quam pater ipsius. Ideo contradixerunt ei, et nuntios ejus remiserunt vacuos a tributis et sine honore, sicut habetur in textu. Alii dicunt, quod Cyrus habuit monarchiam in partibus orientalibus, non in occidentalibus, inter quas dicunt istas in textu expressas fuisse, respectu partium in quibus Cyrus habuit monarchiam. Ad aliud Lyra respondet, quod liber iste ab Hebræis omnino apocryphus reputatur, quia in hac re et aliis multis non videtur bene consonus quibusdam Scripturis canonicis. Potest etiam dici, quod quamvis Samaritani illi favebant regi huic contra Judæos, tamen quia jam tam gravia exegit tributa, fuerunt aversi: vel quamvis aliqui superiores inter ipsos zelabantur pro rege, communes tamen Samaritæ noluerunt regi sic subjici; vel quod de contradictione inductum est, non refertur ad eos, de quibus objectio loquitur, qui quoniam aliorum respectu erant paucissimi, quasi non computantur.
paras.en: Here a twofold question arises. The first: Cyrus, this man's father, was monarch, whence he says: [[1 Esd 1:2|the God of heaven hath given to me all the kingdoms of the earth|Omnia regna terræ dedit mihi Deus cœli]]; and the monarchy had not yet been taken from the Medes and Persians; therefore Cambyses already ruled and was over all these kingdoms. The second: the Samaritans are read in the first book of Esdras to have favoured this king, at whose petition he forbade the repair of the temple, which his father had permitted to be rebuilt[[1 Esd 4:21||]] [the margin gives 1 Esdr. iv, 6–22]. For this is the Artaxerxes to whom the Samaritans wrote, mindful of the salt which they had eaten in the king's palace[[1 Esd 4:14||]]. To the first of these some say that this Cambyses, or Nabuchodonosor, demanded of the aforesaid kingdoms and peoples tributes much heavier than his father had; therefore they refused him, and sent back his messengers empty of tribute and without honour, as is had in the text. Others say that Cyrus held the monarchy in the eastern parts, not in the western, and they say that the lands named in the text were among these western parts, with respect to the parts in which Cyrus held the monarchy. To the other Lyra answers that this book is reckoned wholly apocryphal by the Hebrews, because in this matter and in many others it does not seem to agree well with certain canonical Scriptures. It can also be said that although those Samaritans favoured this king against the Jews, yet because he now exacted such heavy tributes they were turned against him; or that although some of the leading men among them were zealous for the king, the common Samaritans would not be subject to the king in this way; or that what is said of the refusal does not refer to those of whom the objection speaks, who, since they were very few in comparison with the others, are as it were not counted.

paras.t: Ad hos omnes misit nuntios Nabuchodonosor rex Assyriorum: qui omnes uno animo contradixerunt, et remiserunt eos vacuos, et sine honore abjecerunt. Tunc indignatus Nabuchodonosor rex adversus omnem terram illam, id est contra habitatores regnorum et provinciarum illarum, juravit per thronum et regnum suum, per propriam potestatem et jurisdictionem, tanquam per sacra et quædam dignissima, quod defenderet se de omnibus regionibus his, id est, injuriam sibi factam ab illis vindicaret. Nempe ex vehementi superbia, abjectionem legatorum suorum reputavit quasi sui ipsius impugnationem: vel minus dicendo, plus designabat, per quemdam tropum loquendi, qui litotes nuncupatur.
paras.en: [[1:10|To all these Nabuchodonosor king of the Assyrians, sent messengers|Ad hos omnes misit nuntios Nabuchodonosor rex Assyriorum]]: [[1:11|But they all with one mind refused|qui omnes uno animo contradixerunt]], [[1:11|and sent them back empty, and rejected them without honour|et remiserunt eos vacuos, et sine honore abjecerunt]]. [[1:12|Then king Nabuchodonosor being angry against all that land|Tunc indignatus Nabuchodonosor rex adversus omnem terram illam]], that is, against the inhabitants of those kingdoms and provinces, [[1:12|swore by his throne and kingdom|juravit per thronum et regnum suum]], by his own power and jurisdiction, as by sacred and most worthy things, [[1:12|that he would revenge himself of all those countries|quod defenderet se de omnibus regionibus his]] [*defenderet se*, literally *would defend himself*], that is, would avenge the injury done him by them [the scan is badly damaged in these lines; the words of the text are restored from the Vulgate]. For out of vehement pride he counted the rejection of his envoys as an attack on himself: or, by saying less he meant more, by a figure of speech called litotes.

paras.t: Quidam per Nabuchodonosor istum spiritualiter intelligunt diabolum, qui quum plurimos sibi subjecerit, intumescit; sed prosecutio historiæ non videtur ad sensum hujusmodi concordare. Non enim per Arphaxad regem potest intelligi princeps fidelis, sed ipse quoque diabolus: Satanas autem (ut ait Salvator) in se ipsum divisus non est: vel princeps incredulus, qui non resistit diabolo. Similiter gentes idololatræ, quæ in textu leguntur contradixisse Nabuchodonosor regi, non designant plebem fidelium: nec repugnant, sed subduntur, serviuntque diabolo.
paras.en: Some understand this Nabuchodonosor spiritually as the devil, who swells with pride when he has subjected very many to himself; but the course of the history does not seem to agree with a sense of this kind. For King Arphaxad cannot be understood as a faithful prince, but he too would have to be the devil; and Satan (as the Saviour says) is not divided against himself[[Matt 12:26||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the saying is that of Matt 12:26]; or else an unbelieving prince, who does not resist the devil. Likewise the idolatrous nations, which are read in the text to have refused King Nabuchodonosor, do not signify the people of the faithful: nor do they resist the devil, but are subject to him and serve him.

2.title: Declaratio capituli secundi: Anno tertiodecimo regni Nabuchodonosor regis
2.title_en: Explanation of the second chapter: In the thirteenth year of the reign of Nabuchodonosor

paras.t: Hic narratur qualiter Nabuchodonosor iste per suum exercitum præfatas gentes sibi inobedientes vastavit. Nec est difficultas in textu: idcirco nec immorandum, nisi forsan aliquid difficultatis occurrerit.
paras.en: Here it is told how this Nabuchodonosor laid waste by his army the aforesaid nations that were disobedient to him. Nor is there any difficulty in the text: and so there is no need to linger, unless perhaps some difficulty should arise.

paras.t: Anno tertiodecimo regni Nabuchodonosor regis, qui alio nomine vocatus est Artaxerxes et Cambyses, vicesima et secunda die mensis primi: qui a Judæis vocatur Nisan, et est Martius seu Aprilis, quia interdum concurrit cum Martio, aliquando cum Aprili, prout super Genesim et Exodum plenius est expressum; factum est verbum in domo Nabuchodonosor regis Assyriorum, et etiam Medorum atque Persarum, ut defenderet se, id est, […] rex jussit ex parte sui promulgare sententiam, quod vindicaturus se esset de inobedientibus sibi […] ciperent se parare. Vocavitque omnes majores natu, et omnes duces et bellatores suos, et habuit cum eis mysterium, id est secretum, consilii sui; dixitque cogitationem suam in eo esse, ut omnem terram suo subjugaret imperio, id est omnes populos sibi nondum subjectos, præsertim occidentales. Orientales enim sibi jam magna ex parte obediebant.
paras.en: [[2:1|In the thirteenth year of the reign of Nabuchodonosor|Anno tertiodecimo regni Nabuchodonosor]] the king, who by another name was called Artaxerxes and Cambyses, [[2:1|the two and twentieth day of the first month|vicesima et secunda die mensis primi]]: which the Jews call Nisan, and it is March or April, because it sometimes falls with March, sometimes with April, as has been set out more fully on Genesis and Exodus; [[2:1|the word was given out in the house of Nabuchodonosor king of the Assyrians|factum est verbum in domo Nabuchodonosor regis Assyriorum]], and also of the Medes and Persians, [[2:1|that he would revenge himself|ut defenderet se]], that is, […] the king ordered a sentence to be published in his name, that he would take vengeance on those who were disobedient to him […] began to prepare themselves [a line of the scan is unreadable here]. [[2:2|And he called all the ancients, and all the governors, and his officers of war|Vocavitque omnes majores natu, et omnes duces et bellatores suos]], [[2:2|and communicated to them the secret|et habuit cum eis mysterium]], that is, the secret, [[2:2|of his counsel|consilii sui]]; [[2:3|And he said that his thoughts were to bring all the earth under his empire|dixitque cogitationem suam in eo esse, ut omnem terram suo subjugaret imperio]], that is, all the peoples not yet subject to him, especially those of the west. For those of the east were already obedient to him for the most part.

paras.t: Quod dictum cum placuisset […] consiliariis suis, applaudere sibi volentibus, et quia putabant hoc satis faciliter posse impleri, seque ex hoc ampliores divitias ac honores consecuturos, vocavit Holofernem principem militiæ suæ, similem regi suo in omni crudelitate et ambitione, ut infra insinuatur, et dixit ei: Egredere […] quæ respectu terræ Assyriorum sunt in parte occidentali: et contra eos præcipue qui contempserunt imperium meum in tantum, quod legatos meos confusibiliter abjecerunt: ut habetur in fine præcedentis capituli. Non parcet oculus tuus ulli regno, omnemque urbem munitam subjugabis mihi.
paras.en: [[2:4|And when this saying pleased|Quod dictum cum placuisset]] […] his counsellors, who wished to flatter him, and because they thought that this could be accomplished easily enough, and that they would gain greater riches and honours by it, [[2:4|called Holofernes the general of his armies|vocavit Holofernem principem militiæ suæ]], a man like his king in all cruelty and ambition, as is shown below, [[2:5|And said to him: Go out|et dixit ei: Egredere]] […] which, with respect to the land of the Assyrians, are in the western part [two lines of the scan are unreadable here; the verse goes on 'against all the kingdoms of the west']: [[2:5|and against them especially that despised my commandment|et contra eos præcipue qui contempserunt imperium meum]], so far that they cast out my ambassadors with contempt, as is told at the end of the preceding chapter[[Jdt 1:11||]]. [[2:6|Thy eye shall not spare any kingdom, and all the strong cities thou shalt bring under my yoke|Non parcet oculus tuus ulli regno, omnemque urbem munitam subjugabis mihi]].

paras.t: Tunc Holofernes vocavit duces et magistratus virtutis Assyriorum, id est potentium agminum regis. Impii enim quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest, proni sunt ad inquietudines litium et tumultus. Et dinumeravit viros in expeditione, id est in exercitu, seu ad constituendum ex eis exercitum ad prosequendum regis intentum, sicut præcepit ei rex, centum viginti millia peditum pugnatorum. Ex quo patet, quod nec omnes, nec semper pugnabant antiquitus in quadrigis seu curribus, sed quidam pedestres, quidam equestres, sicut et modo: nam subditur, et equites sagittarios duodecim millia, qui in ipso congressu pugnabant sagittando, deinde et aliter. Itaque multo plures erant pedestres. Nam et Vegetius libro de Re militari testatur, quod robur exercitus in peditibus sit consistens. Omnemque expeditionem suam, id est exercitum peditum, fecit præire in, id est eum, multitudinem innumerabilium camelorum, cum his, scilicet victualibus, quæ exercitibus sufficerent copiose, ut essent promptiores ad præliandum. Nempe, ut libro præallegato ait Vegetius, In castris et exercitibus amplius metuenda est fames, quam gladius. Boum quoque armenta, gregesque ovium, quorum non erat numerus. Frumentum ex omni Syria in transitu suo parari constituit. Aurum vero et argentum de domo regis assumpsit multum nimis. Et profectus est ipse, et omnis exercitus cum quadrigis et equitibus, et sagittariis, qui operuerunt faciem, id est superficiem, terræ sicut locustæ, qui vastant et devorant terræ nascentia, sic et illi hominum bona.
paras.en: [[2:7|Then Holofernes called the captains, and officers of the power of the Assyrians|Tunc Holofernes vocavit duces et magistratus virtutis Assyriorum]], that is, of the king's mighty hosts. For the wicked, [[Is 57:20|like the raging sea, which cannot rest|quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]], are prone to the unrest of quarrels and to tumults. [[2:7|and he mustered men for the expedition|Et dinumeravit viros in expeditione]], that is, in the army, or so as to form an army of them to carry out the king's purpose, [[2:7|and the king commanded him|sicut præcepit ei rex]] [the Latin reads *as the king commanded him*], [[2:7|a hundred and twenty thousand fighting men on foot|centum viginti millia peditum pugnatorum]]. From this it is plain that in ancient times not all fought in four-horse chariots or cars, nor always, but some on foot and some on horseback, as now too: for it is added, [[2:7|and twelve thousand archers, horsemen|et equites sagittarios duodecim millia]], who in the encounter itself fought by shooting arrows, and afterwards in other ways as well. So those on foot were far more numerous. For Vegetius too, in his book *On Military Matters*, testifies that the strength of an army consists in its foot soldiers. [[2:8|And he made all his warlike preparations|Omnemque expeditionem suam]], that is, the army of foot, [[2:8|to go before with a multitude of innumerable camels|fecit præire in, id est eum, multitudinem innumerabilium camelorum]] [Denis takes *in* as *eum*, *it*: he made a multitude of innumerable camels go before the army], [[2:8|with all provisions|cum his]], that is, victuals, [[2:8|sufficient for the armies in abundance|quæ exercitibus sufficerent copiose]], that they might be readier for battle. For, as Vegetius says in the book already cited, In camps and armies hunger is more to be feared than the sword. [[2:8|and herds of oxen, and flocks of sheep, without number|Boum quoque armenta, gregesque ovium, quorum non erat numerus]]. [[2:9|He appointed corn to be prepared out of all Syria in his passage|Frumentum ex omni Syria in transitu suo parari constituit]]. [[2:10|But gold and silver he took out of the king's house in great abundance|Aurum vero et argentum de domo regis assumpsit multum nimis]]. [[2:11|And he went forth he and all the army, with the chariots, and horsemen, and archers|Et profectus est ipse, et omnis exercitus cum quadrigis et equitibus, et sagittariis]], [[2:11|who covered the face|qui operuerunt faciem]], that is, the surface, [[2:11|of the earth, like locusts|terræ sicut locustæ]], which lay waste and devour what springs from the earth: so did they too with the goods of men.

paras.t: Quumque pertransisset fines Assyriorum, venit ad magnos montes Ange, qui sunt a sinistro Ciliciæ, ascenditque omnia castella eorum, id est adversariorum, et obtinuit omnem munitionem, id est, loca munita devicit. Effregit autem civitatem opinatissimam, id est famosissimam, vel, ut aliqui habent, opimatissimam, id est opulentissimam, nomine Melothi, quia (ut dicitur) fuit urbs negotiatorum, sicut et Tyrus; prædavitque omnes filios Tharsis, id est, habitatores et cives territorii sic vocati, seu maritimos spoliavit, et filios Ismael, scilicet Agarenos, qui erant contra faciem deserti, id est, in locis eremi, seu ex ejus opposito morabantur, et ad austrum terræ Collon. Et transivit Euphraten, fluvium paradisi, quem per latum transfretavit cum suis, et venit in Mesopotamiam; et fregit, id est, destruxit seu debilitavit, omnes civitates excelsas, quæ erant ibi, a torrente Mambre usquequo perveniatur ad mare Mediterraneum; et occupavit terminos ejus a Cilicia usque ad fines Japhet, qui sunt ad austrum. Abduxitque omnes filios Madian, id est, Madianitas amovit a terra ipsorum et captivavit, aut suo exercitui partim adjunxit ad serviendum, vel adjuvandum: prout infra habetur, quod assumpsit sibi auxiliarios ex gentibus quas devicit; et prædavit omnem locupletationem, id est possessiones et abundantias divitiarum eorum, omnesque resistentes sibi, qui nec jure, seu potius violentia belli acquieverunt subjici ei, occidit in ore gladii. Et post hæc descendit in campos Damasci in diebus messis, videlicet bladis maturis, quando majora potuit ibi damna inferre. Unde subjungitur, et succendit omnia sata, id est blada, omnesque arbores et vineas fecit incidi, id est destrui et excidi.
paras.en: [[2:12|And when he had passed through the borders of the Assyrians, he came to the great mountains of Ange, which are on the left of Cilicia|Quumque pertransisset fines Assyriorum, venit ad magnos montes Ange, qui sunt a sinistro Ciliciæ]]: [[2:12|and he went up to all their castles|ascenditque omnia castella eorum]], that is, of his adversaries, [[2:12|and took all the strong places|et obtinuit omnem munitionem]], that is, he conquered the fortified places. [[2:13|And he took by assault the renowned city|Effregit autem civitatem opinatissimam]], that is, most famous, or, as some have it, *opimatissimam*, that is, most wealthy [the two readings differ by a letter: *opinatissimam*, most renowned, and *opimatissimam*, most opulent], [[2:13|of Melothus|nomine Melothi]], because (as is said) it was a city of merchants, like Tyre too; [[2:13|and pillaged all the children of Tharsis|prædavitque omnes filios Tharsis]], that is, he despoiled the inhabitants and citizens of the territory so called, or the people of the coast, [[2:13|and the children of Ismahel|et filios Ismael]], that is, the Agarenes, [[2:13|who were over against the face of the desert|qui erant contra faciem deserti]], that is, who dwelt in the places of the wilderness or over against it, [[2:13|and on the south of the land of Cellon|et ad austrum terræ Collon]]. [[2:14|And he passed over the Euphrates|Et transivit Euphraten]], the river of paradise[[Gen 2:14||]], which he crossed over its breadth with his men, [[2:14|and came into Mesopotamia|et venit in Mesopotamiam]]; [[2:14|and he forced|et fregit]], that is, destroyed or weakened, [[2:14|all the stately cities that were there|omnes civitates excelsas, quæ erant ibi]], [[2:14|from the torrent of Mambre, till one comes to the sea|a torrente Mambre usquequo perveniatur ad mare]], the Mediterranean; [[2:15|And he took the borders thereof, from Cilicia to the coasts of Japheth, which are towards the south|et occupavit terminos ejus a Cilicia usque ad fines Japhet, qui sunt ad austrum]]. [[2:16|And he carried away all the children of Madian|Abduxitque omnes filios Madian]], that is, he removed the Madianites from their land and made them captive, or partly joined them to his army to serve or to help him, as is told below, that he [[Jdt 3:8|took auxiliaries|assumpsit sibi auxiliarios]] from the nations he had conquered; [[2:16|and stripped them of all their riches|et prædavit omnem locupletationem]], that is, their possessions and the abundance of their wealth, [[2:16|and all that resisted him|omnesque resistentes sibi]], who would not consent to be subjected to him by right, or rather by the violence of war, [[2:16|he slew with the edge of the sword|occidit in ore gladii]]. [[2:17|And after these things he went down into the plains of Damascus in the days of the harvest|Et post hæc descendit in campos Damasci in diebus messis]], that is, when the corn was ripe, when he could do the greater damage there. Hence it is added, [[2:17|and he set all the corn on fire|et succendit omnia sata]], that is, the crops, [[2:17|and he caused all the trees and vineyards to be cut down|omnesque arbores et vineas fecit incidi]], that is, to be destroyed and felled.

paras.t: Ecce quanta scelera ex ambitione nascuntur, et qualiter justus ac sapiens Deus punit unum iniquum per alium. Et cecidit timor illius, id est timor conceptus ex consideratione victoriarum et crudelitatum Holofernis, super omnes inhabitantes terram occidentalem, qui ista perceperunt, et sibi similia fieri metuebant.
paras.en: See how great are the crimes that spring from ambition, and how the just and wise God punishes one wicked man by another. [[2:18|And the fear of them fell|Et cecidit timor illius]] [the Latin has *illius*, *of him*], that is, the fear conceived from considering the victories and cruelties of Holofernes, [[2:18|upon all the inhabitants of the land|super omnes inhabitantes terram]] of the west, who perceived these things and feared that the like would be done to them.

3.title: Explanatio capituli tertii: Tunc miserunt legatos suos
3.title_en: Explanation of the third chapter: Then they sent their ambassadors

paras.t: Narratur jam qualiter plurimæ gentes necessitate et timore compulsæ, subjecerunt se Nabuchodonosor huic.
paras.en: It is now told how a great many nations, driven by necessity and fear, submitted to this Nabuchodonosor.

paras.t: Tunc miserunt legatos suos, universarum urbium et provinciarum, infra nominatarum, reges ac principes, Syriæ scilicet et Mesopotamiæ et Syriæ Sobal, de quibus primo Paralipomenon libro habetur; et erant multum bellicosi, tamen terrore dejecti gratiam petierunt et pacem; et Libyæ atque Ciliciæ: qui venientes ad Holofernem, dixerunt: Desinat indignatio tua circa nos. Melius est enim, id est minus horrendum, ut viventes serviamus Nabuchodonosor regi magno, et subditi simus tibi, quam morientes, cum interitu nostro ipsi servitutis nostræ damna patiamur, id est, non solum efficiamur captivi, sed una cum captivitate protinus occidamur. Mors namque omnium terribilium terribilissimum est, secundum Philosophum. Captivitas vero quæ est mors civilis, non est mors, nisi secundum quid. Omnis civitas nostra, omnisque possessio, omnes montes et colles, et campi, et armenta boum, gregesque ovium et caprarum, equorumque et camelorum, et universæ facultates nostræ atque familiæ, in conspectu tuo sunt, omnia nostra sub lege, id est jussione dispositioneque tua. Nos etiam et filii nostri servi tui sumus; veni nobis pacificus dominus, et utere servitio nostro sicut placuerit tibi.
paras.en: [[3:1|Then the kings and the princes of all the cities and provinces|Tunc miserunt legatos suos, universarum urbium et provinciarum, infra nominatarum, reges ac principes]], named below, [[3:1|of Syria, Mesopotamia, and Syria Sobal|Syriæ scilicet et Mesopotamiæ et Syriæ Sobal]], of which the first book of Paralipomenon tells[[1 Par 19:1||]] (and they were very warlike, yet, cast down by terror, they sought favour and peace), [[3:1|and Libya, and Cilicia sent their ambassadors|et Libyæ atque Ciliciæ]], [[3:1|who coming to Holofernes, said|qui venientes ad Holofernem, dixerunt]]: [[3:2|Let thy indignation towards us cease|Desinat indignatio tua circa nos]], [[3:2|for it is better for us|Melius est enim]], that is, less dreadful, [[3:2|to live and serve Nabuchodonosor the great king, and be subject to thee|ut viventes serviamus Nabuchodonosor regi magno, et subditi simus tibi]], [[3:2|than to die and to perish, or suffer the miseries of slavery|quam morientes, cum interitu nostro ipsi servitutis nostræ damna patiamur]], that is, not only to be made captives, but together with captivity to be killed outright. For death is the most terrible of all terrible things, according to the Philosopher [Aristotle]; while captivity, which is civil death, is not death except in a certain respect. [[3:3|All our cities and our possessions, all mountains and hills, and fields, and herds of oxen, and flocks of sheep, and goats, and horses, and camels, and all our goods, and families are in thy sight|Omnis civitas nostra, omnisque possessio, omnes montes et colles, et campi, et armenta boum, gregesque ovium et caprarum, equorumque et camelorum, et universæ facultates nostræ atque familiæ, in conspectu tuo sunt]]: [[3:4|Let all we have be subject to thy law|omnia nostra sub lege tua]], that is, to thy bidding and disposing. [[3:5|Both we and our children are thy servants|Nos etiam et filii nostri servi tui sumus]]; [[3:6|Come to us a peaceable lord, and use our service as it shall please thee|veni nobis pacificus dominus, et utere servitio nostro sicut placuerit tibi]].

paras.t: Tunc descendit de montibus, et obtinuit civitatem munitam regnorum jam prædictorum, et omnem populum inhabitantem terram provinciarum istarum, seu quosdam de omnibus. Vel per modum hyperbolicæ locutionis est accipiendum, ad innuendum quod valde multos subdidit sibi, sicut in Daniele Nabuchodonosor rex Chaldæorum legitur cunctis regnis ac provinciis terræ imperasse. Et in Esdræ libro asserit Cyrus: Omnia regna terræ dedit mihi Deus. Juxta quem tropum Scribæ et Pharisæi leguntur dixisse de Christo: Ecce totus mundus abiit post eum. De universis autem urbibus, quæ sic sine resistentia subdiderunt se ei, assumpsit auxiliarios viros fortes, quia plus credidit illis.
paras.en: [[3:7|Then he came down from the mountains|Tunc descendit de montibus]], [[3:7|and made himself master of every city|et obtinuit civitatem munitam]] [Denis reads *the fortified city*; the margin gives the reading *omnem*, every] of the kingdoms already named, [[3:7|and all the inhabitants of the land|et omnem populum inhabitantem terram]] of those provinces, or some out of all. Or it is to be taken as a hyperbolic way of speaking, to hint that he subdued very many to himself, as in Daniel Nabuchodonosor king of the Chaldeans is read to have ruled over all the kingdoms and provinces of the earth[[Dan 4:19||]] [the margin is hard to read here; apparently Dan. iv]. And in the book of Esdras Cyrus asserts that God [[1 Esd 1:2|hath given to me all the kingdoms of the earth|Omnia regna terræ dedit mihi Deus]]. According to this figure the Scribes and Pharisees are read to have said of Christ: [[John 12:19|Behold, the whole world is gone after him|Ecce totus mundus abiit post eum]]. [[3:8|And from all the cities|De universis autem urbibus]], which thus submitted to him without resistance, [[3:8|he took auxiliaries valiant men|assumpsit auxiliarios viros fortes]], because he trusted them more.

paras.t: Tantusque metus provinciis illis incubuit, ut universarum urbium habitatores principes, et honorati simul cum populis, exirent obviam venienti, excipientes eum cum coronis et lampadibus, ducentes choros in tympanis et tibiis. Nec tamen ista facientes, ferocitatem pectoris ejus mitigare in toto potuerunt, quamvis eum tam honorifice acceperunt, exeundo obviam venienti: exeundo, inquam, cum coronis, id est sertis, in signum triumphorum ipsius, et lampadibus seu luminaribus, quasi ad honorem præclaræ et splendidæ potestatis ac sapientiæ suæ. Nam et civitates eorum quasdam destruxit, vel partim muros evertendo, vel totaliter eas incendendo; et lucos eorum succidit, id est loca amœna arboribus consita, in quibus suas idololatrias atque luxurias exercebant: quod non fecit zelo veri Dei, sed ob causam quæ subditur.
paras.en: [[3:9|And so great a fear lay upon all those provinces, that the inhabitants of all the cities, both princes and nobles, as well as the people, went out to meet him at his coming|Tantusque metus provinciis illis incubuit, ut universarum urbium habitatores principes, et honorati simul cum populis, exirent obviam venienti]], [[3:10|And received him with garlands, and lights|excipientes eum cum coronis et lampadibus]], [[3:10|and dances, and timbrels, and flutes|ducentes choros in tympanis et tibiis]]. [[3:11|And though they did these things, they could not for all that mitigate the fierceness of his heart|Nec tamen ista facientes, ferocitatem pectoris ejus mitigare in toto potuerunt]] altogether, though they received him so honourably, going out to meet him at his coming: going out, I say, with garlands [*coronis*, crowns], that is, wreaths, in sign of his triumphs, and with lamps or lights, as if in honour of his glorious and splendid power and wisdom. [[3:12|For he both destroyed their cities|Nam et civitates eorum quasdam destruxit]], some of them, either partly by overthrowing their walls or wholly by burning them; [[3:12|and cut down their groves|et lucos eorum succidit]], that is, pleasant places planted with trees, in which they practised their idolatries and lusts: which he did not out of zeal for the true God, but for the reason that follows.

paras.t: Præceperat enim illi Nabuchodonosor rex, ut omnes deos terræ exterminaret, id est templa seu fana et cultum illorum, videlicet ut ipse solus deus diceretur ab his nationibus, quæ potuissent Holofernis potentia subjugari. Neque prosperitas stulti illius perdidit eum, inducendo eum ad tam insanissimam sceleratissimamque superbiam, quod jussit sibi divinum exhiberi honorem, non obstante quod mortalem se sciret. Talis fuit et Caius Cæsar, et Herodes percussus ab angelo. Ideo infinita sapientia Dei decentissime ipsum dejecit per feminam, et regno eum privavit in se ipso ac posteris, ita quod filium regni successorem non habuit. Circa quod scribit quidam, quod secundum Latinos ei successit Darius filius Hystaspis: sed in Scholastica historia verius recitatur, quod ante Darium illum duo ei successerunt, quamvis modico regnaverint tempore, scilicet Ireneides, et post eum frater ejusdem.
paras.en: [[3:13|For Nabuchodonosor the king had commanded him to destroy all the gods of the earth|Præceperat enim illi Nabuchodonosor rex, ut omnes deos terræ exterminaret]], that is, their temples or shrines and their worship, [[3:13|that he only might be called God by those nations which could be brought under him by the power of Holofernes|videlicet ut ipse solus deus diceretur ab his nationibus, quæ potuissent Holofernis potentia subjugari]]. And the prosperity of that fool destroyed him [the scan seems to read *Neque*, which the sense does not allow; perhaps *Itaque* or *Atque*], leading him on to so utterly insane and wicked a pride that he commanded divine honour to be shown him, although he knew himself to be mortal. Such too was Caius Caesar, and Herod, who was struck by an angel[[Acts 12:23||]]. Therefore the infinite wisdom of God most fittingly cast him down by a woman, and deprived him of the kingdom in himself and in his posterity, so that he had no son to succeed him in the kingdom. On this a certain writer says that according to the Latins Darius the son of Hystaspes succeeded him; but in the Scholastic History it is more truly related that before that Darius two succeeded him, though they reigned only a short time, namely Ireneides, and after him his brother.

paras.t: Pertransiens autem Syriam Sobal sibi nunc subjugatam, et omnem Apameam, omnemque Mesopotamiam, venit ad Idumæos in terram Gabaa. Gabaa non est hic nomen civitatis terræ promissionis, de qua Saul fuit, sed loci in regno Edom. Et Scythopoli; accepitque civitates eorum, vel bello, aut ex voluntaria seu potius coacta præbitione ipsorum. Quæ enim ex timore fiunt, partim sunt voluntaria, partim involuntaria, secundum Philosophum, sicut projectio mercium in mare. Et sedit ibi, id est, in territorio illo moratus est, per triginta dies, consumens et devorans bona terræ illius. Sic et Balac rex ait: Egressus est populus ex Ægypto sedens contra me. Talis etenim demoratio quandoque designatur nomine sessionis, aliquando nomine stationis; interdum verbo jacendi aut faciendi, ut in Jacobo: Faciemus ibi annum. In quibus diebus adunari præcepit universum exercitum virtutis, id est potestatis suæ, volens cum potestate et gloria proficisci ad ulteriora. Multi autem de exercitu ejus discurrebant hinc inde ad prædandum et male agendum.
paras.en: [[3:14|And when he had passed through all Syria Sobal|Pertransiens autem Syriam Sobal]], now subjugated to him, [[3:14|and all Apamea, and all Mesopotamia|et omnem Apameam, omnemque Mesopotamiam]], [[3:14|he came to the Idumeans into the land of Gabaa|venit ad Idumæos in terram Gabaa]]. Gabaa is not here the name of the city of the land of promise from which Saul came[[1 Kings 10:26||]], but of a place in the kingdom of Edom. And to Scythopolis [the reading is uncertain: the scan seems to give *Scythopoli*]; and [[3:15|he took possession of their cities|accepitque civitates eorum]], either by war, or by their own willing, or rather forced, surrender. For things done out of fear are partly voluntary and partly involuntary, according to the Philosopher, like the throwing of goods into the sea. [[3:15|and stayed there|Et sedit ibi]] [*sedit*, literally *sat*], that is, he lingered in that territory, [[3:15|for thirty days|per triginta dies]], consuming and devouring the goods of that land. So too King Balac says: [[Num 22:5|Behold a people is come out of Egypt|Egressus est populus ex Ægypto]], [[Num 22:5|sitting over against me|sedens contra me]]. For such a stay is sometimes designated by the name of sitting, sometimes by that of standing; sometimes by the verb of lying or of making, as in James: [[Jas 4:13|there we will spend a year|Faciemus ibi annum]] [literally *we will make a year there*]. [[3:15|in which days he commanded all the troops of his army to be united|In quibus diebus adunari præcepit universum exercitum virtutis]], that is, of his power [*virtutis*, of his might], wishing to go on to further parts with power and glory. And many of his army ran about here and there to plunder and do harm.

paras.t: Nabuchodonosor iste et Holofernes recte dicuntur tenuisse Antichristi figuram, qui omnia devastabit: et qui subjecerunt se Holoferni, significant eos qui ex timore subdent se Antichristo.
paras.en: This Nabuchodonosor and Holofernes are rightly said to have borne the figure of Antichrist, who will lay all things waste: and those who submitted to Holofernes signify those who out of fear will submit to Antichrist.
